title: Health & Wellness Spas
one_liner: U.S. spas have moved past the pandemic rebound into steadier, price-and-visit-led growth, with medical aesthetics, hotel/resort wellness and membership models carrying the upside.
overview: The U.S. spa industry reached a record $23.5 billion in 2025, up 4.2% from $22.5 billion in 2024, according to ISPA's 2026 Big Five statistics. Visits rose to 191 million in 2025, nearly matching the 192 million pre-pandemic peak in 2019, while revenue per visit increased to $123.10 in 2025 from $120.30 in 2024. Growth is no longer mainly a reopening rebound; it is coming from higher spend per visit, broader wellness routines, premium skin care, resort/hotel spa demand, memberships and medical-aesthetic add-ons. The sector remains fragmented: in 2025 there were 22,060 U.S. spa locations, including 17,200 day spas, 2,210 resort or hotel spas and 1,820 medi-spas. Operators face persistent constraints from licensed labor availability, wage pressure, facility capacity and state-by-state rules for massage, esthetics and medical services.

baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline followed the 2020 collapse and 2021 reopening rebound, with demand still rebuilding from the 192 million spa visits recorded in 2019.

how_it_makes_money: Spas earn revenue from massages, facials, body treatments, hydrotherapy, salon and beauty services, memberships, packages, gift cards, retail skin-care products, wellness experiences and, where legally supervised, medical-aesthetic services such as injectables, lasers, peels, body contouring and light therapy. Resort and hotel spas also monetize travelers and day-pass guests, while franchise chains rely heavily on recurring member visits and standardized add-on sales.
cost_structure: Labor is the central cost because services require licensed massage therapists, estheticians, nail technicians, front-desk staff, managers and, for medical spas, clinical supervision. Other major 2025 costs include rent or hotel revenue-share arrangements, treatment rooms and wet-area maintenance, laundry, professional products, medical devices, insurance, booking software, marketing, franchise royalties and compliance. In ISPA's 2026 study, one in three respondents cited staffing as the single biggest challenge, while 2025 profitability softened outside resort/hotel spas: 60% of non-resort/hotel spas reported profit above 10%, down from 67% in 2024.
major_players: Massage Envy: nearly 1,000 U.S. franchised locations in 2026 and more than 240 million services delivered since 2002
Hand & Stone Massage and Facial Spa: 600+ locations nationwide in 2026, built around membership massage, facial and add-on services
Woodhouse Spa: upscale day-spa franchise focused on massage, facials, body treatments and retail
Canyon Ranch: destination wellness resorts and retreats serving the premium wellness-travel segment
Miraval Resorts & Spas: Hyatt-owned resort wellness brand serving high-end travel and experiential wellness demand
Ideal Image and other med-spa chains: medical-aesthetic providers competing for injectables, laser, body contouring and recurring skin-care spend
current_dynamics: Demand is solid but maturing. 2025 revenue growth of 4.2% trailed 2024 growth of 5.8%, showing the post-pandemic rebound is normalizing. Visits grew 1.8% in 2025, while average spend per visit grew 2.3%, so pricing, premium add-ons and mix are doing more of the work. Inflation still matters: BLS reported personal care services prices up 4.4% year over year in June 2026. Capacity is tight because licensed labor and treatment-room availability limit appointment supply. Resort and hotel spas benefit from wellness travel and higher revenue per visit, while day spas depend more on memberships, local repeat traffic and weekday utilization. Medical spas are a fast-growing adjacent competitor and partner category, with AmSpa reporting the U.S. medical spa industry above $17 billion in 2026 and growing by more than $1 billion per year.
whats_growing: Medical aesthetics, LED light therapy, premium facials, head-spa treatments, wellness travel, hotel/resort day access, memberships, retail skin care, personalized add-ons and technology-enabled booking are growing. ISPA's full 2026 study reported LED light therapy offered by 62% of day spas, 58% of resort/hotel spas and 74% of other spas in 2025, while head-spa treatments were offered by 29% of day spas and 33% of resort/hotel spas. Massage Envy reported 2025 momentum in hot stone services, full-body LED light therapy, CBD, cupping, advanced skin care and a limited robotic massage test.
whats_shrinking: The easy reopening rebound is shrinking: 2025 revenue growth slowed to 4.2% from 5.8% in 2024. Contract labor is losing share in the spa workforce, with ISPA's 2025 Big Five chart showing contract employees down 6.5% from January 2024 to January 2025. Profit cushions outside resort/hotel spas also narrowed in 2025, with the share reporting profit above 10% falling to 60% from 67% in 2024. Purely appointment-only, single-service formats are under pressure when they lack memberships, retail, add-ons, medical supervision or hotel/resort demand channels.
recent_developments: 2025-03: ISPA reported 2024 U.S. spa revenue of $22.5 billion, up 5.8%, with 187 million visits.
2025-06: ISPA's full 2025 study showed average revenue per spa establishment of $1.024 million in 2024 and 21,980 locations.
2026-01: ISPA named 2025 Innovate Award winners across spa operations, technology, products and experience categories.
2026-02: ISPA Research Foundation released a playbook on pre-visit spa anticipation and guest journey design.
2026-03: ISPA released 2026 Big Five statistics showing 2025 revenue of $23.5 billion and 191 million visits.
2026-07: ISPA's full 2026 U.S. Spa Industry Study reported 17,200 day spas, 2,210 resort/hotel spas and 1,820 medi-spas in 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but slower than the rebound years. Revenue should keep expanding as consumers treat massage, skin care and recovery as repeat self-care, but growth will depend on utilization, pricing discipline, premium services and staffing. Resort/hotel spas are positioned to outperform because wellness travel supports higher spend per visit. Day spas need memberships, local marketing and efficient scheduling to offset wage, rent and product-cost pressure. Medical spas will keep pulling consumer dollars toward injectables, lasers, weight-loss and skin rejuvenation, raising both growth opportunities and regulatory risk. The biggest constraint through 2026 is not demand alone but whether operators can hire licensed providers, modernize facilities and add higher-margin services without weakening service quality or compliance.
themes: premium skin care and LED treatments

title: Health Food & Supplement Store Franchises
one_liner: Franchised vitamin, supplement and health-food stores remain a small specialty retail niche, benefiting from wellness demand but losing share to e-commerce, mass merchants and omnichannel chains.
overview: Health Food & Supplement Store Franchises are mature specialty retailers built around repeat purchases, staff guidance, franchisor sourcing programs and brand trust. The 2022 baseline was $824.8 million of revenue, and the industry likely remained below $1.0 billion in 2026 because franchise-format specialty stores capture only a narrow slice of the much larger U.S. supplement market. Demand fundamentals are favorable: U.S. dietary supplement sales reached $72.88 billion in 2025, up 5.5% in 2025, and CRN reported 75% of U.S. adults used dietary supplements in 2024. The constraint is channel mix: health and personal care retail sales reached $40.241 billion in May 2026, but nonstore retailers and mass merchants continue to absorb wellness spending through subscriptions, marketplace search, private label and aggressive price comparison.

key_stats.market_size: 2026E U.S. franchise-store revenue: about $839 million, based on the 2022 IBIS baseline and slow 2022-2027 forecast trajectory
key_stats.growth: 2026E industry revenue growth: about 0.5%; 2025 U.S. dietary supplement market growth: 5.5%
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 baseline EBIT margin: 5.4%; 2027 baseline forecast EBIT margin: 5.2%
key_stats.broader_market: 2025 U.S. dietary supplement sales: $72.88 billion; 2025 vitamins share: 26.7%; 2025 specialty ingredients share: 22.4%; 2025 sports nutrition share: 15.6%
key_stats.consumer_usage: 2024 U.S. adult supplement usage: 75%; 2024 median monthly supplement spend among users: $50
key_stats.retail_context: May 2026 health and personal care store sales: $40.241 billion, seasonally adjusted

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from in-store and digital sales of vitamins, minerals, herbal products, sports nutrition, protein powders, weight-management products, probiotics, specialty supplements, health foods, functional beverages and ancillary wellness items. Franchisees pay or share economics with franchisors in exchange for brand rights, product sourcing, training, store systems, marketing support and operating playbooks. Margin depends on private-label mix, repeat-purchase loyalty, vendor rebates, staff-assisted upselling and the ability to hold premium prices against Amazon, Walmart, Target, Costco and subscription brands.
cost_structure: The largest cost is merchandise purchases from supplement, packaged-food and functional-beverage suppliers, followed by store labor, rent, franchise fees, payment processing, local marketing, freight and shrink. In the 2022 baseline, wages were $133 million, equal to about 16.1% of 2022 revenue, while EBIT profit was $45 million, equal to a 5.4% 2022 margin. Inflation, freight volatility and promotional price matching pressured 2025-2026 store margins, while franchisor purchasing leverage and private-label supplements partly offset those pressures.
major_players: The Vitamin Shoppe as a major specialty-channel competitor
Sunmed and CBD-focused wellness franchise retailers
Independent local health-food and supplement franchise operators
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is healthier at the product level than at the store-franchise level. Supplement consumption is mainstream, specialty products such as magnesium, prebiotics, ashwagandha, probiotics, collagen and sports nutrition are growing, and large consumer companies are paying strategic premiums for credible supplement brands. However, franchise stores face a crowded shelf: mass retailers, grocery chains, Amazon, TikTok Shop, direct-to-consumer brands and practitioner-led channels all compete for the same wellness basket. Store formats need trained associates, local community credibility, click-and-collect, subscriptions and exclusive products to defend traffic.
whats_growing: Growth is strongest in 2025-2026 for specialty ingredients, healthy-aging formulas, women’s health, gut health, magnesium, prebiotics, collagen, creatine, GLP-1-adjacent nutrition, protein, functional beverages, gummies and personalized supplement routines. Franchise systems with exclusive labels, loyalty data, local coaching and omnichannel fulfillment are better positioned than stores relying mainly on commodity multivitamins.
whats_shrinking: Commodity vitamins, undifferentiated third-party brands, COVID-era immunity spikes, mall-based traffic, low-service supplement shelves and products with weak substantiation are losing momentum. Price-sensitive consumers can compare the same SKU online in 2026, and regulators are increasing pressure on disease claims, misleading advertising and unlawful ingredients.
recent_developments: February 2024: GNC announced a Raleigh market franchise expansion that transferred 5 corporate stores to a franchisee and said nearly one-third of GNC locations were independently operated.
October 2024: CRN reported 75% of U.S. adults used dietary supplements in 2024, with 2024 median monthly user spending of $50.
May 2025: Kingswood Capital and Performance Investment Partners completed the acquisition of The Vitamin Shoppe from Franchise Group and returned Sharon Leite as CEO.
July 2025: FDA issued warning letters over 7-hydroxymitragynine products and stated 7-OH is not lawful in dietary supplements.
March 2026: Nutrition Business Journal data reported U.S. dietary supplement sales of $72.88 billion in 2025, up 5.5% in 2025.
August 2026: P&G agreed to acquire supplement maker Thorne for $3.8 billion, highlighting strategic interest in premium wellness and personalized supplements.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is modestly positive but below broader supplement-market growth. A reasonable 2026 estimate is about $839 million in franchise-store revenue, compared with the 2022 baseline of $824.8 million and the 2027 baseline forecast of $842.3 million. Demand will be supported by aging consumers, sports nutrition, preventive wellness and daily supplement routines, but channel leakage to nonstore retail, big-box private label and DTC subscriptions will cap revenue growth. Margin upside depends on private-label mix, franchisor buying power, labor scheduling, loyalty programs and compliance discipline around health claims.
themes: Big-box and online retailers compress price
Private label and exclusives protect margin
Healthy aging and GLP-1-adjacent nutrition reshape assortments

title: Healthcare Consultants
one_liner: Healthcare consultants sell strategy, operations, technology, reimbursement, compliance and transformation advice to providers, payers, life-sciences companies, employers and public agencies.
overview: Healthcare consultants advise hospitals, physician groups, insurers, pharmaceutical companies, medical-device makers, employers and government agencies on strategic planning, financial performance, revenue cycle, human resources, IT modernization, compliance, M&A, supply chain and clinical operating models. The baseline IBIS file described a growth-stage industry driven by healthcare reform, rising total health expenditure, Medicare and Medicaid complexity, EHR adoption and pressure to reduce care delivery costs. Current 2025-2026 data points to a larger and more technology-intensive market, with US healthcare consulting services estimated at $12.55 billion in 2025 and projected at $13.67 billion in 2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $12.55 billion US healthcare consulting services revenue
key_stats.growth: 2025: +9.2% year over year; 2026: +8.9% projected year over year
key_stats.healthcare_spending_backdrop: 2024: US national health expenditure was $5.3 trillion, up 7.2%, equal to 18.0% of GDP; 2025-2034: CMS projects 5.4% average annual NHE growth

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $9.71 billion US healthcare consulting services revenue
baseline_2022.baseline_context: 2020 IBIS baseline revenue was $7.0 billion with a 2020 profit margin of 9.8%; the older file projected 2025 revenue of $8.8 billion before later market estimates revised the opportunity higher.

how_it_makes_money: Firms earn fees through project-based strategy and transformation engagements, retainers, implementation support, outcome-linked performance contracts, managed advisory arrangements and specialist work in revenue cycle, digital health, analytics, cybersecurity, compliance, transactions, workforce planning and clinical operations. Baseline 2020 service mix was led by strategic management at 58.8% of revenue, financial management and operations at 17.8%, other services at 11.4%, HR and benefits at 7.1%, and IT strategy at 4.9%; by 2025, digital and technology consulting was identified as the fastest-growing segment.
cost_structure: The largest cost is skilled labor: partners, clinicians, former payer executives, actuaries, data scientists, regulatory specialists, implementation managers and offshore delivery teams. Other material costs include 2025-2026 software platforms, data subscriptions, cybersecurity controls, cloud environments, subcontractors, sales and proposal costs, insurance, travel and office overhead. Margins are supported by premium pricing for scarce healthcare expertise but pressured by 2025-2026 wage competition, AI investment, client demand for measurable ROI and outcome-based fee risk.
current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled forward by 2025-2026 margin pressure across providers and payers, growth in Medicare and government-sponsored spending, AI and automation projects, payer denial pressure, value-based care redesign, cybersecurity needs and a renewed focus on outpatient and home-based care models. At the same time, clients are scrutinizing fees more closely, pushing consultants to pair advice with implementation capacity, data assets, software partnerships and measurable performance improvement.
whats_growing: Digital and technology consulting, AI-enabled workflow redesign, revenue cycle management, denials prevention, payer-provider contracting, interoperability, cybersecurity, cloud and data governance, value-based care, Medicare Advantage strategy, outpatient growth strategy, physician enterprise performance improvement, home health and hospice growth support, and private-equity portfolio optimization are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Standalone diagnostic strategy decks, non-implementation advisory work, generic EHR optimization, small undifferentiated boutiques, projects tied to financially weak inpatient-only providers, low-tech compliance work and consulting that cannot show 2025-2026 ROI are losing share. Demand tied to skilled nursing and lower-growth outpatient categories is more constrained than demand tied to home, hospice, ASC, HST and revenue-cycle transformation.
recent_developments: 2026-07: Ken Research estimated the US healthcare consulting services market at $12.55 billion in 2025 and projected $13.67 billion in 2026.
2026-06-24: CMS released 2025-2034 NHE projections showing 5.4% average annual health spending growth versus 4.1% GDP growth.
2026-04-30: McKinsey reported that 60% of surveyed US care-delivery RCM leaders expected to change outsourcing strategy over the next two years.
2026-02-10: Kaufman Hall reported hospital adjusted year-to-date operating margin closed 2025 at 1.3%, with expenses, bad debt and charity care rising.
2026-01-12: McKinsey projected health services and technology revenue pools to grow 8% annually from 2024 to 2029, supporting consulting and implementation demand.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but more demanding: revenue should keep expanding as healthcare clients fund transformation projects to offset reimbursement pressure, labor inflation, payer friction and regulatory complexity. Growth is strongest where consultants combine healthcare domain expertise with AI, automation, analytics, revenue-cycle execution and measurable financial outcomes. Risks include client budget cuts, slower private insurance enrollment growth, higher uninsured and self-pay exposure, consulting-fee compression, cybersecurity liability and competition from software vendors, internal transformation teams and tech-enabled services firms.
themes: Revenue cycle management and denial prevention

title: Healthcare Staff Recruitment Agencies
one_liner: Healthcare staffing agencies place temporary and permanent nurses, physicians, allied health professionals and executives into hospitals, clinics, post-acute and home-based care settings.
overview: This industry earns fees by recruiting, credentialing and placing healthcare workers for client facilities. The baseline IBIS file reported 2020 revenue of $21.8 billion and projected 2025 revenue of $28.9 billion, but the pandemic-driven travel-nurse spike pushed broader SIA-tracked US healthcare staffing revenue to $72.5 billion in 2022 before normalizing to an estimated $39.4 billion in 2025 and $40.2 billion in 2026. Demand is tied to hospital volumes, healthcare spending, clinician vacancies, licensing and credentialing speed, and client willingness to pay agency bill rates. The market remains fragmented, although national firms have advantages in MSP/VMS relationships, compliance, candidate pools and technology-enabled matching.

key_stats.market_size: $39.4 billion in 2025 US healthcare staffing revenue; $40.2 billion forecast for 2026, based on SIA forecast cited in AMN Healthcare's 2026 investor materials.
key_stats.growth: -6.0% in 2025 versus $41.9 billion in 2024; +2.0% forecast in 2026 versus 2025, calculated from SIA figures cited by AMN.
key_stats.travel_nurse_trend: Travel nurse revenue declined 12.1% in 2025, while average bill rate edged from $90.13 in 2024 to $90.54 in 2025, according to the 2026 SIA/NATHO survey summarized by Becker's.
key_stats.healthcare_spending_driver: US national health expenditures grew 7.2% to $5.3 trillion in 2024; CMS projects 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth averaging 5.4% per year.
key_stats.rn_labor_driver: BLS projected 189,100 registered nurse openings per year over 2024-2034, with 5% employment growth.
key_stats.physician_labor_driver: AAMC projected a US physician shortage of 13,500 to 86,000 physicians by 2036 in its 2024 report.

baseline_2022.market_size: $72.5 billion in 2022 US healthcare staffing industry revenue, based on SIA forecast cited by AMN Healthcare.
baseline_2022.growth: +41.1% in 2022 versus $51.4 billion in 2021, calculated from SIA figures cited by AMN.
baseline_2022.context: 2022 was an abnormal peak year because crisis-level travel nurse demand and bill rates followed the 2020-2021 COVID-19 capacity shock.

how_it_makes_money: Agencies charge healthcare clients bill rates or placement fees. Temporary staffing generates the largest revenue stream because clinicians stay on the agency payroll and the client pays a marked-up hourly or daily bill rate covering wages, benefits, payroll taxes, compliance, recruiting and margin. Locum tenens and allied staffing are usually billed per shift, day or assignment. Permanent placement and executive search generate one-time fees tied to a candidate's accepted salary or a retained-search contract. Larger firms also earn revenue from managed service provider programs, vendor management systems, recruitment process outsourcing, credentialing support and workforce analytics.
cost_structure: The largest 2025 cost is clinician compensation and related payroll costs; AMN Healthcare's 2025 cost of revenue was 71.7% of revenue and gross profit was 28.3%. Selling, general and administrative costs were 21.7% of AMN revenue in 2025, reflecting recruiter labor, sales teams, compliance, credentialing, housing and travel coordination, technology platforms, insurance and corporate overhead. Industry margins are pressured when bill rates fall faster than pay packages, when hospitals shift demand to internal float pools, or when MSP/VMS fees compress supplier markups.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is in post-pandemic normalization rather than broad collapse. Hospitals reduced premium travel-nurse use after the 2022 peak, and travel-nurse revenue continued declining in 2025, but bill rates stabilized and contingent labor remains part of workforce planning. Locum tenens, advanced practice provider coverage, allied health, home health, hospice and tele-staffing are more resilient growth pockets. Client margin pressure keeps procurement disciplined, favors MSP/VMS programs and increases demand for transparent pricing, vendor consolidation and faster credentialing.
whats_growing: Locum tenens is growing because physician shortages persist and rural, emergency, psychiatry, primary care and specialty coverage gaps remain hard to fill. Home health, hospice, ambulatory sites and PACE programs are growing as care shifts outside inpatient hospitals. Technology-enabled matching, credentialing automation, workforce analytics, internal-agency support and tele-staffing are growing as buyers seek lower cost and faster fill times. Permanent placement and interim leadership are recovering where hospitals need durable workforce fixes rather than repeated premium assignments.
whats_shrinking: Pandemic-era travel nursing is shrinking from the 2022 peak as bill rates normalize, billed hours fall and hospitals use internal float pools, local contracts and stricter agency utilization controls. Per diem nursing is exposed where facilities can cover shifts with internal labor. Pure-play suppliers without MSP access, compliance scale or specialized clinician pools face pricing pressure. Public staffing companies exposed to nurse and allied staffing reported 2025 revenue declines, including AMN's 8% consolidated decline and Cross Country's continued segment pressure.
recent_developments: 2024-12-04: Aya Healthcare agreed to acquire Cross Country Healthcare for about $615 million in cash.
2025-02-20: The FTC issued a second request for information on the Aya-Cross Country transaction under HSR review.
2025-12-04: Cross Country terminated the Aya merger agreement and said Aya owed a $20 million termination fee.
2026-01-13: Grand View Research estimated the US healthcare staffing market at $45.48 billion in 2025 and forecast 6.98% CAGR for 2026-2033.
2026-05-26: Becker's reported SIA/NATHO survey findings that aggregate travel nurse revenue declined 12.1% in 2025 while bill rates stabilized.
2026-06-24: CMS published 2025-2034 health spending projections with national health expenditure growth averaging 5.4% per year.
outlook: Revenue is likely to return to modest growth in 2026 after the 2022-2025 correction, with SIA figures cited by AMN implying $40.2 billion in 2026 revenue, up 2.0% from 2025. The medium-term outlook is supported by aging demographics, 2024-2034 RN openings, 2036 physician shortages and 2025-2034 healthcare spending growth. The main constraint is hospital cost pressure: buyers will keep limiting premium travel labor, renegotiating bill rates and routing spend through MSP/VMS channels. Agencies with deep specialty pools, locum tenens scale, compliance infrastructure and technology-led fulfillment should outperform generalist suppliers.
themes: Allied health and home-based care demand
one_sentence: After the 2021-2022 travel-nurse surge, US healthcare staffing is smaller but stabilizing as health systems keep using contingent labor to cover persistent clinician shortages, census volatility and specialty gaps.

title: Healthcare and Social Assistance in the US
one_liner: A $4.3 trillion-plus provider sector driven by aging demand, public and private insurance reimbursement, wage pressure and care shifting from hospitals into outpatient, home and value-based settings.
overview: The sector is the broad operating backbone of US care delivery: physician offices, outpatient centers, hospitals, nursing homes, residential care, home health, child and family services, and related social assistance. Census Quarterly Services Survey data show 2025 sector revenue of $4.314 trillion, up 8.4% from $3.981 trillion in 2024, with Q1 2026 revenue at $1.107 trillion, or a $4.428 trillion annualized run rate. Demand is structurally supported by population aging, chronic disease, expanded insured coverage and high healthcare price inflation, while margins are constrained by clinical labor shortages, wage inflation, payer mix, drug and supply costs, and reimbursement policy changes.

how_it_makes_money: Providers earn revenue by billing private insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, self-pay patients, employers, households and government programs for medical care, residential care, home health, behavioral health, diagnostics, outpatient procedures, emergency services and social support services. CMS reported 2024 national health expenditures of $1.645 trillion from private health insurance, $1.118 trillion from Medicare, $931.7 billion from Medicaid and $556.6 billion out of pocket, showing how reimbursement is split across public programs, commercial coverage and patients. Employer coverage remains a major commercial funding channel, with KFF reporting 2025 average annual premiums of $9,325 for single coverage and $26,993 for family coverage.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant operating cost because care delivery depends on clinicians, nurses, aides, technicians, administrators and social workers; BLS reported June 2026 average hourly earnings of $36.19 for all employees in NAICS 62 and Q2 2026 private-industry compensation growth of 3.8% year over year. Hospitals also carry heavy drug, medical supply, purchased services, malpractice insurance, IT, rent, depreciation and interest costs; Census QSS reported Q1 2026 hospital expenses of $429.8 billion. Profitability varies widely: outpatient, specialty and value-based care assets can be attractive, while hospitals, nursing homes and social assistance providers face pressure from staffing intensity, uncompensated care and government reimbursement rates.
major_players: HCA Healthcare: 2025 revenue of $75.6 billion, with 2025 same-facility revenue up 6.6%.
UnitedHealth Group Optum Health: 2025 revenue of $102.0 billion, reflecting the scale of payer-owned care delivery and physician enablement.
Kaiser Permanente: major integrated nonprofit insurer-provider system with hospitals, medical groups and health plans.
CommonSpirit Health: large nonprofit hospital and ambulatory care system.
Ascension: large nonprofit Catholic health system with hospital, clinic and post-acute assets.
Tenet Healthcare: investor-owned hospital and ambulatory surgery operator.
current_dynamics: Demand is rising faster than the pre-pandemic IBIS baseline because utilization normalized, prices increased and coverage remained broad. The mix continues to move toward ambulatory surgery, outpatient diagnostics, home health, virtual care, behavioral health and managed Medicare models. At the same time, providers face persistent staffing shortages, higher wage and benefit costs, pressure from Medicare and Medicaid rate-setting, insurer prior authorization disputes, and higher drug costs tied partly to specialty medicines and GLP-1 adoption. Policy is a central swing factor: CY2026 Medicare Advantage payments are set to rise, physician fee schedule rules are changing reimbursement mechanics, and marketplace enrollment remains near record levels at 23.1 million 2026 plan selections.
whats_growing: Ambulatory care, home health, behavioral health integration, Medicare Advantage-funded care models, digital and remote monitoring, outpatient surgery, senior care demand, revenue-cycle automation and payer-provider partnerships are growing. CMS projects 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth of 5.4% per year on average, with Medicare spending growing 7.7% annually and retail prescription drug spending the fastest major category at 5.7% annually.
whats_shrinking: Relative share is shrinking for inpatient-only care models, low-margin standalone nursing facilities, uncompensated emergency-room care exposure, small independent practices without payer leverage, and parts of fee-for-service care that are being pushed into value-based contracts or lower-cost outpatient settings. Medicaid redeterminations and eligibility operations remain a risk for providers with high low-income patient exposure, while employers and insurers are pushing back against premium increases and high-cost networks.
recent_developments: 2025-01-17: CMS reported 24.2 million consumers selected ACA Marketplace coverage for plan year 2025.
2025-04-07: CMS finalized CY2026 Medicare Advantage and Part D policies, projecting MA payments to plans up 5.06% from 2025 to 2026.
2025-10-22: KFF reported 2025 employer family premiums rose 6% to $26,993 and single premiums rose 5% to $9,325.
2025-10-31: CMS finalized the CY2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, including separate APM and non-APM conversion factors and telehealth policy updates.
2026-03-27: CMS reported 23.1 million consumers selected or were automatically re-enrolled in 2026 Marketplace coverage.
2026-06-11: Census QSS showed Q1 2026 NAICS 62 revenue of $1.107 trillion, up 0.4% from Q4 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but cost-sensitive. Revenue should keep expanding on demographic demand, chronic disease prevalence, Medicare growth, near-record exchange enrollment and ongoing price increases, with Q1 2026 QSS data implying a $4.428 trillion annual run rate. Real growth will be slower than nominal growth because wage, benefits, drugs and supply inflation absorb much of the increase. The best-positioned operators are scaled systems with payer contracts, outpatient capacity, technology-enabled labor productivity and value-based risk capabilities; weaker operators are exposed to staffing shortages, uncompensated care, Medicaid policy shifts and reimbursement lag.
one_sentence: Healthcare and Social Assistance in the US includes ambulatory providers, hospitals, nursing and residential care, and social assistance organizations whose 2025 revenue grew strongly as utilization, prices, Medicare Advantage payments, ACA enrollment and labor costs all remained elevated.
